analysis.investment_thesis: Aadhar Housing Finance occupies a compelling position in India's massive affordable housing deficit, posting a 33.4% net profit CAGR over 6 years — the kind of earnings compounding Fisher respects. However, ROE of 16.9% remains below my 20% threshold and the business model demands perpetual external financing, limiting the compounding flywheel.
key_strengths: Net profit CAGR of 33.4% over 6 years (FY19–FY25: INR 162 Cr → INR 912 Cr) — exceptional earnings growth
Operating income CAGR of 21.3% over 3 years with clearly expanding margin trend; gross margin near 98% reflects pure-play lending economics
Affordable housing is a structurally large and government-supported TAM; Blackstone-backed promoter brings institutional discipline and capital access
key_risks: ROE of 16.9% and ROCE of 11.4% are below Fisher's 20% ROE threshold, suggesting capital is not yet being deployed with exceptional efficiency
Debt/Equity of 2.55 and total debt of INR 16,322 Cr creates vulnerability to credit cycle turns or rising cost of funds

Negative operating cash flow every single year (0/5) is structural for HFCs but means the business requires constant external financing to grow — the quality of loan book and NPA trajectory is the key unknown
red_flags: Revenue CAGR of 16.1% over 6 years is below Fisher's 20%+ growth threshold — growth is good but not exceptional
Zero FCF generation across all 5 years — entirely dependent on debt markets to fund loan book expansion
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Aadhar Housing Finance delivers the profit growth numbers Fisher admires — a 33.4% net profit CAGR is elite — and the affordable housing segment (average ticket sizes under INR 10 lakh) addresses a market that India's formal banking system has chronically under-served. Revenue grew from INR 1,266 Cr (FY19) to INR 3,108 Cr (FY25) with accelerating momentum, and total assets have expanded to INR 25,083 Cr. The forward P/E of 16.2x is modest for this growth rate.

The central concern from a Fisher lens is that HFCs are fundamentally leveraged intermediaries: there is no proprietary innovation moat, no R&D pipeline, and growth is gated by capital markets access. The ROE of 16.9% — while improving — does not yet reflect the 20%+ return profile I expect from a truly exceptional business. I hold, awaiting evidence that ROE can breach 20% as the loan book seasons and operating leverage kicks in.
